seltz.snippet:

During the night of 15–16 August 1943 German police and SS units threw a cordon around the ghetto in Białystok. In the morning it was announced that all its inhabitants – some 30,000 people – were to report with their luggage to an assembly square, from where they would be “resettled”. For the Jewish underground this was the signal it had been awaiting for months. Several hundred young people, armed with about twenty-five rifles, about a hundred pistols and bottles of petrol and acid, attacked the Germans at the ghetto fence on Smolna Street. They wanted to breach it and lead as many people as possible out to the nearby Knyszyn Forest.

The plan failed. German superiority was overwhelming, and the weapons and ammunition were enough for a few hours’ fighting at most. Resistance at isolated points nevertheless continued for several more days. The leaders of the uprising, Mordechai Tenenbaum and Daniel Moszkowicz, died in the ghetto – according to the findings of post-war historians they took their own lives when their ammunition ran out. The ghetto ceased to exist, and its inhabitants were deported to camps where most of them perished. The Krasowo-Częstki massacre was a Nazi German pacification operation carried out on 17 July 1943 against the village of Krasowo-Częstki in the Białystok region of occupied Poland , resulting in the deaths of 257 civilians—97 children, 89 women, and 71 men—through shooting and burning them alive in a barn , after which the entire settlement was razed. [[1]](#ref-1) [[2]](#ref-2) The perpetrators, units of the SS, gendarmerie , and Wehrmacht , acted in retaliation for the killing of eight German gendarmes in a skirmish with Polish Home Army partisans on 11 July near the village, herding nearly all inhabitants together before executing them en masse. [[1]](#ref-1) [[3]](#ref-3) Only 24 villagers survived, having escaped or been absent during the assault. [[1]](#ref-1) This event formed part of broader German anti-partisan reprisals in the region during the summer of 1943 , targeting rural Polish communities suspected of supporting resistance activities, and stands as one of the deadliest such actions in the annexed Białystok area. Postwar investigations and commemorations, including the construction of a chapel at the site of the barn and annual memorials listing the victims, have preserved accounts from survivors and official records confirming the scale of the civilian toll, with no evidence of combatant presence among those killed.
